title: Primality testing: Miller-Rabin (randomized) vs AKS (deterministic)
problem_statement: Given an integer N >= 0, decide whether N is prime.

algorithms.name: Miller-Rabin
algorithms.idea: Write N - 1 = 2^s d. A random base a is a witness of compositeness unless a^d = 1 or a^(2^j d) = -1 mod N for some j < s. At least 3/4 of bases are witnesses for any odd composite.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(k n^3) bit operations for k rounds with schoolbook multiplication (Õ(k n^2) with fast multiplication)
algorithms.correctness: Rabin 1980: a composite passes one round with probability <= 1/4; primes always pass (one-sided error). Error <= 4^(-k).

algorithms.name: AKS
algorithms.idea: Deterministic polynomial-identity test (X + a)^N = X^N + a mod (X^r - 1, N).
algorithms.time_complexity: Õ(n^(21/2)) as proven in AKS 2004; Õ(n^6) for the Lenstra-Pomerance variant

relationship: Both are polynomial. Miller-Rabin is far faster but randomized (PRIMES in coRP); AKS removes the randomness unconditionally at the price of a much larger polynomial degree.

sources.title: Riemann's hypothesis and tests for primality
sources.venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences 13(3), 300-317

sources.authors: Agrawal, M.; Kayal, N.; Saxena, N.
sources.title: PRIMES is in P

verification.method: Both implementations agree with each other and with a sieve oracle on random n-bit integers, n = 0..20 (AKS up to 16 bits). Miller-Rabin runs 32 rounds, so a false 'prime' has probability <= 4^-32 per composite.

caveats: The V1 run of a randomized algorithm is itself probabilistic (failure probability <= 4^-32 per composite tested). Miller's 1976 deterministic variant (bases up to O(log^2 N)) is polynomial only assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
notes: Also an instance of the general derandomization question (BPP vs P); compare polynomial-identity-testing (staging), where deterministic polynomial time is open.
